title: NyQuil and Alcohol: Is It Safe? Does NyQuil Have Alcohol?
excerpt: Can you drink on NyQuil, or take it after drinking? How doxylamine and acetaminophen interact with alcohol, how much alcohol NyQuil itself contains, how long to wait, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Can you drink on NyQuil? How its sedating antihistamine and acetaminophen interact with alcohol, how much alcohol NyQuil contains, and how long to wait.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** don't drink alcohol while you're taking NyQuil, and don't take NyQuil to knock yourself out after a night of drinking. NyQuil Cold & Flu combines three drugs, and alcohol makes two of them riskier. The **acetaminophen** (the active ingredient in Tylenol) adds to the work alcohol already puts on your liver. The **doxylamine** is a sedating antihistamine, and alcohol is a sedative too, so together they can make you far drowsier, clumsier, and slower to react than either one alone. And yes, the classic NyQuil liquid contains alcohol itself: it lists alcohol as an inactive ingredient, at about 10%. That small amount isn't the main danger, but it surprises a lot of people.

**The quick rules:** Pick one or the other tonight, not both. If you've been drinking, wait until you're fully sober before taking NyQuil, and skip it entirely after a heavy night. If you've taken NyQuil, don't drink until the next day. Never take Tylenol or another acetaminophen product on top of NyQuil. If you drink 3 or more drinks a day on a regular basis, ask a doctor or pharmacist before using NyQuil at all, because the label says so. If you think you or someone else took too much acetaminophen, call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US) right away, even if they feel fine.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and the information printed on US over-the-counter labels. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and the medicines you take. **Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before combining NyQuil and alcohol if** you drink heavily most days, have liver disease, breathing problems such as asthma, COPD, or sleep apnea, glaucoma, or trouble urinating from an enlarged prostate, or if you take an antidepressant, a sleep medicine, an anxiety medicine, an opioid, or any other prescription drug. **Get help now (call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 in an emergency) if** someone who mixed NyQuil and alcohol can't be woken up, is breathing slowly or irregularly, is vomiting while very drowsy, or is confused; or if you may have taken more than the labeled dose of acetaminophen, or you notice nausea, vomiting, pain under your right ribs, yellow skin or eyes, or dark urine.

## What's Actually in NyQuil

NyQuil is a Vicks brand, and the name covers several products. The most common one, **Vicks NyQuil Cold & Flu**, comes as a liquid and as LiquiCaps. Each standard adult dose combines three active ingredients:

| Ingredient | What it does | Per one adult dose (30 mL liquid or 2 LiquiCaps) |
|---|---|---|
| Acetaminophen | Pain reliever and fever reducer | 650 mg |
| Dextromethorphan HBr | Cough suppressant | 30 mg |
| Doxylamine succinate | Sedating antihistamine (for sneezing, runny nose, and the "Quil" sleepiness) | 12.5 mg |

The adult label says to take a dose every 6 hours and **no more than 4 doses in 24 hours**. That's up to 2,600 mg of acetaminophen a day from NyQuil alone, before you count anything else you take.

Other versions change the formula. **NyQuil Severe** adds phenylephrine, a decongestant. **NyQuil HBP**, made for people with high blood pressure, skips the decongestant and uses a different antihistamine. **ZzzQuil** is a separate sleep aid that contains diphenhydramine (the drug in Benadryl) and no acetaminophen. Formulas change over time and vary by country, so the Drug Facts box on *your* package is the only list that counts.

## Does NyQuil Have Alcohol in It?

Yes, the regular NyQuil liquid does. Alcohol is listed among its inactive ingredients, and the liquid has long been described as about 10% alcohol. It's there as a solvent that helps keep the ingredients dissolved, which is common in liquid cough and cold medicines.

The **LiquiCaps do not list alcohol** as an ingredient, and Vicks also sells alcohol-free liquid versions. If avoiding alcohol completely matters to you, read the inactive ingredients on the box rather than going by the product name, because different NyQuil products in the same aisle can differ.

### How much alcohol is in a dose?

Not much in practical terms. A 30 mL dose at 10% alcohol works out to about 3 mL of pure alcohol. A US standard drink contains roughly 17 to 18 mL (14 grams) of pure alcohol. So one dose of NyQuil liquid holds a small fraction of one drink, very roughly a sixth.

That won't make you drunk, and it won't meaningfully raise your blood alcohol level. Where it can matter:

- **You avoid alcohol for a medical reason.** Some medicines, such as the antibiotic metronidazole and the drug disulfiram, can cause a bad reaction with even small amounts of alcohol. Pregnancy is another situation where people often prefer to avoid any. Ask a pharmacist which alcohol-free option fits.
- **You avoid alcohol for personal or religious reasons.** The LiquiCaps or an alcohol-free liquid solve the problem.
- **A breath test shortly after a dose.** Alcohol sitting in your mouth right after you swallow a liquid medicine can briefly register on a breath test, the same way mouthwash can. Rinsing your mouth and waiting usually clears it. This is about mouth alcohol, not real intoxication.

Here's the important part: **the alcohol inside NyQuil is not the reason NyQuil and drinking are a bad mix.** The real problems are the acetaminophen and the doxylamine. A product with zero alcohol still carries both risks.

## Why NyQuil and Alcohol Don't Mix

### 1. Doxylamine plus alcohol: stacked sedation

Doxylamine is an older, "first-generation" antihistamine. Unlike newer allergy drugs such as cetirizine or loratadine, it crosses easily into the brain, where it blocks histamine signals that help keep you awake. That's why NyQuil makes you sleepy. Doxylamine is also the active ingredient in some over-the-counter sleep aids sold on its own.

Alcohol slows the brain down through different routes, mainly by boosting the calming chemical GABA and dampening the excitatory chemical glutamate. When two drugs slow the brain down by different routes, their effects add up, and the result can be stronger than you'd guess from either one. That's why the NyQuil label tells you to **avoid alcoholic drinks** and warns that alcohol, sedatives, and tranquilizers may increase drowsiness.

In real life, stacked sedation looks like:

- Much heavier drowsiness than usual, and falling asleep faster and harder
- Poor coordination, stumbling, and a higher chance of falls, especially getting up at night to use the bathroom
- Slower reactions and poor judgment, which makes driving dangerous even if you feel "fine"
- Confusion or memory gaps
- In larger amounts, slowed breathing and being hard to wake

Doxylamine also lasts a long time. Its half-life (the time it takes your body to clear half of it) has been measured at around 10 hours in healthy adults, and longer in older people. Many people feel groggy the next morning after a single dose. That matters if you plan to drink the following day, or if you took NyQuil late at night and have to drive early.

Older antihistamines also have "anticholinergic" effects, meaning they block a chemical messenger involved in many automatic body functions. That's what causes the dry mouth, constipation, blurry vision, and trouble urinating some people get. Alcohol can add to the confusion side, and older adults are especially sensitive to it.

### 2. Acetaminophen plus alcohol: extra work for your liver

Every standard dose of NyQuil Cold & Flu contains 650 mg of acetaminophen. Your liver clears most of it safely, but a small slice is turned into a toxic by-product called NAPQI. Normally the liver neutralizes NAPQI right away with an antioxidant called glutathione.

Regular heavy drinking tilts that balance in two ways. It boosts the liver enzyme (CYP2E1) that makes NAPQI, and it lowers glutathione stores. Skipping meals lowers glutathione too, and people who are sick or hungover often aren't eating. When NAPQI is made faster than glutathione can clean it up, liver cells are damaged.

That's why US over-the-counter acetaminophen products, NyQuil included, carry a liver warning: severe liver damage may occur if you take more than the maximum daily amount, take it with other drugs containing acetaminophen, or have **3 or more alcoholic drinks every day** while using the product. Acetaminophen is the leading cause of acute liver failure in the United States, and many of those cases are accidental: a little too much, over several days, from more than one product, often alongside alcohol.

For the full explanation, including how much is too much and the warning signs, see our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol).

### 3. Dextromethorphan plus alcohol: more dizziness

Dextromethorphan (often shortened to DXM) is a cough suppressant that works in the brain. At normal doses it's mild, but it can cause dizziness and drowsiness on its own, and alcohol adds to both. At very high doses, far above the label, DXM causes intoxication and is sometimes misused; combining that with alcohol is dangerous. At the label dose, the main takeaway is simple: it's one more ingredient pushing in the same sleepy, unsteady direction.

DXM also has an important drug interaction: it should not be taken with MAO inhibitors (an older class of antidepressants), and combining it with certain other antidepressants can raise the risk of a serious reaction called serotonin syndrome. If you take any antidepressant, ask a pharmacist before using NyQuil, whether or not you're drinking. Our [cough medicine and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/cough-medicine-and-alcohol) covers DXM and other cough ingredients in more detail.

### 4. You're sick

This one gets overlooked. You take NyQuil because you have a cold or flu. Alcohol dehydrates you, disrupts the deep sleep your body uses to recover, and can blunt parts of your immune response. Even setting the drug interactions aside, drinking while you're sick tends to make you feel worse for longer.

## Can You Drink After Taking NyQuil? How Long to Wait

There's no official waiting period printed on the label. The label's instruction is simply to avoid alcoholic drinks while using the product. A sensible approach for most healthy adults:

- **If you took NyQuil tonight, don't drink tonight.** The doxylamine is at its strongest in the first several hours.
- **Wait until the next day at the earliest.** Because doxylamine lingers, many people still feel some sedation 8 hours or more after a dose. If you still feel groggy, that's your answer: wait longer.
- **If you're taking NyQuil repeatedly over several days, skip drinking until you're done with it.** Repeated doses mean steady acetaminophen and steady antihistamine in your system.

A single drink many hours after a single dose is unlikely to cause a crisis in a healthy adult. But it's an easy combination to avoid, and the point of NyQuil is to help you rest and recover, which alcohol works against.

## Can You Take NyQuil After Drinking?

This is the more common situation, and the riskier one: you've been out, you're coming down with something or just want to sleep, and NyQuil is in the cabinet.

**After a heavy night, don't.** You'd be adding a sedating antihistamine on top of alcohol that's still in your blood, plus acetaminophen to a liver that's still processing that alcohol, often on an empty stomach. The person most at risk is someone who's quite drunk, takes NyQuil to sleep, and then vomits while too sedated to wake up and turn over. Choking on vomit is a real danger of mixing sedatives with heavy drinking.

**After a drink or two, wait.** Give your body time to clear the alcohol first. As a rough guide, the body clears about one standard drink per hour, though this varies a lot between people. If you'd hesitate to drive, you're not ready for a sedating medicine either.

**When you do take it, take one standard dose.** Not a double dose to "make sure it works," and not alongside any other cold, flu, sleep, or pain product unless you've checked the labels.

## NyQuil for a Hangover: Not a Good Idea

People sometimes reach for NyQuil to sleep off a hangover or to handle a headache plus queasy stomach. It's a poor fit:

- **It doesn't treat a hangover.** There's no good evidence that any NyQuil ingredient helps the main hangover symptoms beyond the acetaminophen dulling a headache. The cough suppressant and antihistamine aren't doing anything useful for you.
- **The acetaminophen comes at a bad time.** If you drink heavily on a regular basis, the morning after is when your liver may be least able to handle extra acetaminophen.
- **More sedation on a foggy day.** You may already feel slow and unsteady. Doxylamine adds to that, and it can still be in your system hours later.
- **Hangover symptoms can hide early overdose signs.** Early acetaminophen poisoning often looks like nausea, sweating, and feeling unwell, which is also what a hangover feels like.

If a headache is the main problem, a single standard dose of a plain pain reliever, taken after you've eaten and the alcohol has cleared, is a simpler choice than a multi-symptom product. Our guide on [Advil or Tylenol for a hangover](/never-hungover/advil-or-tylenol-for-hangover) compares the options and their trade-offs.

## Using NyQuil to Sleep After Drinking

This deserves its own section because it's so common. Alcohol makes you fall asleep faster, but it breaks up your sleep in the second half of the night, which is why you often wake at 3 or 4 a.m. after drinking. Some people try to fix that with NyQuil or another sleep aid. That's the riskiest version of this combination: two sedatives, taken specifically to deepen sleep, while alcohol is still being processed.

Safer ways to handle a bad night of sleep after drinking:

- Stop drinking a few hours before bed and switch to water.
- Eat something before bed if you haven't.
- Keep the room cool and dark, and skip screens if you wake up.
- Accept a rough night rather than chasing it with a sedative.

If you're curious why alcohol wrecks sleep in the first place, our article on [alcohol and REM sleep](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-rem-sleep-complete-scientific-analysis-2025) explains what's going on. And if you're wondering about lighter sleep aids, see our guide to [melatonin and alcohol](/never-hungover/melatonin-and-alcohol), which isn't a sedative in the same way but still isn't a great match with drinking.

## NyQuil vs. DayQuil With Alcohol

Both carry the same acetaminophen warning and both contain dextromethorphan. The difference is the third ingredient:

| | NyQuil Cold & Flu | DayQuil Cold & Flu |
|---|---|---|
| Acetaminophen per dose | 650 mg | 650 mg |
| Cough suppressant | Dextromethorphan | Dextromethorphan |
| Third ingredient | Doxylamine (sedating antihistamine) | Phenylephrine (decongestant) |
| Main extra concern with alcohol | Heavy sedation, impaired coordination and breathing at high amounts | Can nudge up heart rate; still adds to liver load |
| Liquid contains alcohol? | Regular liquid lists alcohol as an inactive ingredient | Check the label; formulas vary |

The sedation is what makes NyQuil the more hazardous of the two with alcohol. A common mistake is taking DayQuil during the day and NyQuil at night, then adding Tylenol for a headache. That's three sources of acetaminophen. Count them. Our full breakdown of [DayQuil and alcohol](/never-hungover/dayquil-and-alcohol) covers the daytime formula.

## The Hidden-Acetaminophen Trap

The single most useful habit with NyQuil is checking every other product you take for acetaminophen. It's also in:

- DayQuil and most store-brand "cold and flu" or "multi-symptom" products
- "PM" pain relievers such as Tylenol PM
- Combination headache pills such as Excedrin
- Some prescription painkillers, such as hydrocodone or oxycodone combined with acetaminophen
- Some powdered hot-drink cold remedies

On labels, look for **acetaminophen**, **APAP**, or **paracetamol**. The daily limit covers all of them combined. If you're already taking NyQuil, don't add Tylenol on top.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You're at higher risk from the NyQuil-and-alcohol combination if you:

- Drink **3 or more drinks most days**, or binge regularly
- Have **liver disease**, hepatitis, fatty liver, or elevated liver enzymes
- Have **breathing problems** such as asthma, COPD, or sleep apnea, since stacked sedation can worsen breathing during sleep
- Are **an older adult**, because older people clear doxylamine more slowly and are more prone to confusion and falls
- Take **other sedating medicines**: prescription sleep aids, anxiety medicines such as benzodiazepines, opioid painkillers, muscle relaxers, gabapentin, or other antihistamines
- Take an **antidepressant**, especially an MAO inhibitor, because of the dextromethorphan interaction
- Have **glaucoma** or **trouble urinating** from an enlarged prostate, which older antihistamines can worsen

If any of these apply, have a short conversation with a pharmacist before using NyQuil, drinking or not. For a broader look at how common medicines interact with alcohol and supplements, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help Right Away

> **When to get help now.** Call 911 if someone who mixed NyQuil (or any sleep aid) with alcohol **can't be woken up, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has blue or gray lips, is having a seizure, or is vomiting while barely conscious.** Turn them on their side so they can't choke, and stay with them. These are signs of dangerous sedation or alcohol poisoning, and they need emergency care, not sleeping it off. Call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US) if you may have taken more than the labeled amount of acetaminophen, took several acetaminophen products and aren't sure of the total, or feel unwell after a few days of NyQuil plus drinking, even if symptoms seem mild.

Acetaminophen poisoning is sneaky. People can feel fairly normal for the first day even after a dangerous amount, and the damage shows up later. Signs that can point to liver injury:

- Nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, sweating, or feeling generally ill (easy to mistake for a hangover or the flu itself)
- Pain or tenderness under the right side of your ribs
- Yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes
- Dark urine or pale stools
- Confusion, unusual sleepiness, or easy bruising or bleeding

Hospitals have an effective antidote for acetaminophen overdose, intravenous N-acetylcysteine (NAC), and it works best when started early. That's why calling right away matters more than waiting to see whether symptoms appear.

## Simple Ways to Handle a Cold and a Social Calendar

If you're sick and have plans that involve drinking, the easiest options are:

- **Skip the drinks this time.** A non-alcoholic beer or a mocktail lets you show up without the interaction worries.
- **Treat symptoms one at a time.** If you only have a stuffy nose or only a cough, a single-ingredient product often makes more sense than a multi-symptom one, and it may avoid acetaminophen or sedation entirely. A pharmacist can point you to the right one in a minute.
- **Use non-drug comfort measures.** Fluids, warm drinks, honey for a cough (for adults and children over one year), saline nose spray, and rest.
- **Keep NyQuil for nights you're not drinking.** That's what it's designed for.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

To be clear up front: **no supplement makes it safe to combine NyQuil and alcohol.** There's no good evidence that DHM, or anything else you can buy, protects against acetaminophen liver injury or counters the sedation from doxylamine. Follow the NyQuil label regardless.

For nights when you *are* drinking and not taking cold medicine, some people use DHM (dihydromyricetin), a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven, and it's no substitute for drinking less and eating and hydrating well. If you want to try it, popular picks include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and if you take any prescription medicine, check with your pharmacist first. For the habits with the best evidence, see [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## The Bottom Line

- NyQuil and alcohol is a bad mix mainly because of **doxylamine** (stacked sedation) and **acetaminophen** (extra liver load), not the small amount of alcohol in the liquid.
- The regular NyQuil liquid does contain alcohol, about 10%, which is roughly a sixth of a standard drink per dose. LiquiCaps and alcohol-free versions avoid it.
- Don't drink on a night you take NyQuil, and don't take NyQuil after a heavy night of drinking or to treat a hangover.
- Never stack NyQuil with Tylenol, DayQuil, or other acetaminophen products. Count every source.
- If you have 3 or more drinks most days, ask a doctor before using NyQuil.
- If someone mixed them and can't be woken or is breathing poorly, call 911. If there's any chance of an acetaminophen overdose, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 right away.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking NyQuil?**

It's best not to. NyQuil Cold & Flu contains doxylamine, a sedating antihistamine that adds to alcohol's drowsiness and loss of coordination, and acetaminophen, which adds to the work alcohol puts on your liver. The label tells you to avoid alcoholic drinks while using it. If you drink 3 or more drinks a day on a regular basis, ask a doctor or pharmacist before using NyQuil at all.

**Does NyQuil have alcohol in it?**

The regular NyQuil liquid does. It lists alcohol as an inactive ingredient, at about 10%, where it helps keep the medicine dissolved. A 30 mL dose holds roughly a sixth of a standard drink's worth of alcohol, which won't make you drunk. NyQuil LiquiCaps don't list alcohol, and Vicks sells alcohol-free liquid versions. Check the inactive ingredients on your package if you need to avoid alcohol completely.

**How long after taking NyQuil can I drink alcohol?**

There's no official waiting period on the label, which simply says to avoid alcohol while using the product. Because doxylamine lasts a long time (its half-life is around 10 hours in healthy adults), a sensible approach is to wait until the next day at the earliest and longer if you still feel groggy. If you're taking NyQuil over several days, skip drinking until you've finished.

**Can I take NyQuil after drinking?**

Not after a heavy night. You'd be adding a sedating antihistamine on top of alcohol still in your blood, which can deepen sedation and raise the risk of choking if you vomit while asleep, plus acetaminophen to a liver that's still processing alcohol. After a drink or two, wait until you're fully sober, then take a single standard dose and no other acetaminophen products.

**Is NyQuil good for a hangover?**

No. There's no good evidence that NyQuil's ingredients help a hangover beyond the acetaminophen dulling a headache, and the doxylamine adds more grogginess to an already foggy day. The acetaminophen also comes at a bad time if you drink heavily on a regular basis. If a headache is the main problem, a single dose of a plain pain reliever after you've eaten is a simpler choice.

**What happens if you mix NyQuil and alcohol?**

Most often, much heavier drowsiness, dizziness, poor coordination, and slowed reactions than either would cause alone, which makes falls and driving dangerous. With larger amounts, breathing can slow and a person can become hard to wake. Repeated use alongside heavy drinking can also raise the risk of acetaminophen liver damage. Call 911 if someone can't be woken, is breathing slowly, or is vomiting while barely conscious.

**Will NyQuil show up on a breathalyzer?**

A dose of NyQuil liquid contains only a small amount of alcohol and won't meaningfully raise your blood alcohol level. But alcohol left in your mouth right after swallowing a liquid medicine can briefly register on a breath test, much like mouthwash. Rinsing your mouth and waiting usually clears it. The bigger issue is that NyQuil itself can impair driving, so don't drive after taking it.

**Is NyQuil or DayQuil worse with alcohol?**

NyQuil is generally the riskier of the two because its doxylamine adds strong sedation on top of alcohol. Both contain 650 mg of acetaminophen per dose and carry the same liver warning, and both contain dextromethorphan. Taking DayQuil by day, NyQuil at night, and Tylenol on top is an easy way to exceed the daily acetaminophen limit, so count every source.
